title: Changing “false” to “true”: How I Discovered an Email Verification Bypass Through Mass Assignment
summary_en: An attacker bypassed the mandatory email verification process by sending a PATCH request that manually updated their account's verification status flag to 'true'.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a Mass Assignment vulnerability in the profile update API. Mass Assignment occurs when an application takes user-provided data and automatically saves it to a database record without filtering which fields are allowed to be changed. In this case, the endpoint at /mobify/proxy/api/customer/.../customers/{customerId} accepted the 'c_isCustomerVerified' field from the user's request. Because the server did not use an allowlist (a list of safe fields like 'name' or 'address'), it allowed the user to overwrite a sensitive internal status flag that should only be controlled by the system.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher created a new account on redacted.com using a temporary email address.
2. Upon logging in, the site displayed a verification wall, blocking access to profile editing and order tracking until the email link was clicked.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher used Burp Suite (a tool that intercepts and inspects web traffic) to monitor the background communication between the browser and the server.
4. They identified a GET request (a request to fetch data) used to load the user's profile details.
GET /mobify/proxy/api/customer/.../customers/{customerId}?siteId=redacted HTTP/1.1
Why: This endpoint (a specific web address for an API) returns the current state of the user's account in the database.
5. The researcher examined the JSON response (a text-based data format used by APIs) and found a specific flag (a true/false indicator).
{
 "customerId": "12345",
 "email": "testuser@example.com",
 "c_isCustomerVerified": "false"
}
Why: The 'c_isCustomerVerified' label with the value 'false' tells the website that this user has not yet clicked the email link.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher sent the request to Burp Repeater (a tool for modifying and re-sending requests) and changed the method from GET to PATCH.
PATCH /mobify/proxy/api/customer/shopper-customers/v1/organizations/redacted_org/customers/{customerId}?siteId=redacted
Why: A PATCH request is used to update existing information on a server.
7. The researcher added a JSON payload (the data sent in the body of the request) to the PATCH request, manually setting the verification flag to true.
{
 "c_isCustomerVerified": "true"
}
Why: The researcher is testing if the server blindly accepts this instruction to change its internal record of the user's status.
8. The server responded with a '200 OK' status code, indicating the update was successful.

IMPACT
9. To confirm the exploit, the researcher sent the original GET request again.
GET /mobify/proxy/api/customer/.../customers/{customerId}?siteId=redacted
Why: To see if the server now reports the user as verified.
10. The response confirmed the change: '"c_isCustomerVerified": "true"'.
11. The researcher refreshed the browser, and the verification wall disappeared, granting full access to the account without ever opening an email inbox.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site called 'target.example' where users can sign up for a free trial. When you view your profile, the site sends a request to 'GET /api/v1/me' and receives this JSON: {'username': 'newbie', 'is_premium_subscriber': false}. To test for Mass Assignment, an attacker would try to send a 'PUT' or 'PATCH' request to the same endpoint with a modified payload: {'is_premium_subscriber': true}. If the server is vulnerable, it will update the user's database record, granting them paid features for free because the developer forgot to tell the code: 'Only allow users to change their username, never their subscription status.'
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always inspect the JSON responses of profile or settings pages for interesting boolean (true/false) flags like 'isVerified', 'isAdmin', or 'can_access_beta'. If you find one, try to send that same flag back to the server using a PUT or PATCH request. A common beginner mistake is assuming that because a field isn't visible in a web form, it can't be changed; however, APIs often listen for more fields than the UI shows. Look for 'hidden' parameters in the documentation or by observing the traffic of different user roles.

excerpt: When you sign up on most shopping websites, they ask you to click a link in your email before you can edit your profile or track orders. title: The Illusion of Instant Block
summary_en: A blocked user could maintain their session to perform administrative actions and unblock themselves by exploiting a mass assignment vulnerability in the profile update endpoint.

lesson.cause: The application suffered from two main implementation flaws. First, it failed to invalidate active sessions upon account deactivation, meaning the server only checked the 'blocked' status during the initial login (authentication) but not for subsequent actions (authorization). Second, the profile update endpoint was vulnerable to Mass Assignment, where the server-side code mapped incoming JSON data directly to the database model. This allowed the researcher to identify the 'status' parameter in a server response and then send it back with a modified value. Because the application did not filter which fields a user could update, it blindly accepted the new status.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Researcher identifies a feature that allows Admins to block or deactivate users.
2. Researcher sets up two accounts: an Admin account and a target User account.
DISCOVERY
3. Admin blocks the User account to test if the restriction is immediate.
4. User checks if their session (a digital 'handshake' that keeps you logged in) is still valid by attempting to browse the site.
EXPLOITATION
5. User sends an HTTP request (a message sent from your computer to a server) to change their profile name while supposedly blocked.
POST /api/profile/edit HTTP/1.1 ... {"name":"Hacker"}
6. Why: The server fails to verify the account's status for this specific endpoint (a specific URL that performs an action), allowing the request to succeed.
7. User attempts to delete other admins using the active session to prove high impact.
POST /api/admin/delete-user HTTP/1.1 ... {"id":"admin_id"}
8. Why: The session remains fully privileged because the server didn't revoke (cancel or invalidate) the session when the block occurred.
9. User observes the response (data sent back by the server after a request) from the name-change request.
{"name":"Hacker", "status":"BLOCKED"}
10. Why: The response contains a 'status' parameter (a label for a piece of data) which reveals the internal field name used to track the block.
11. User sends a new request including the 'status' parameter set to 'ACTIVE' to attempt to unblock themselves.
POST /api/profile/edit HTTP/1.1 ... {"name":"Hacker", "status":"ACTIVE"}
12. Why: This exploits Mass Assignment (when a program takes a list of data and saves it to a database without checking permissions for each item).
IMPACT
13. User verifies they have successfully unblocked themselves by checking the Admin panel.
14. Why: The server blindly accepted the user-provided 'status' value and updated the account record in the database.
lesson.example: A fictional website target.example allows users to update their profile. The server-side code looks like this: 'user.update(params[:user_data])'. An attacker notices that when they view their profile, the server sends back a JSON response: '{"username":"bob", "is_admin":false}'. The attacker sends a request: 'PUT /api/settings {"user_data": {"is_admin":true}}'. Because the server takes the entire 'user_data' block from the request and saves it to the database without checking if 'is_admin' should be editable by the user, the attacker becomes an administrator.
lesson.takeaway: Always test if a session survives an account status change like being blocked, deactivated, or changing a password. Look for sensitive fields in JSON responses, such as 'role', 'status', 'permissions', or 'is_admin', and try to include them in 'update' or 'edit' requests. A common variant is 'Over-posting', where you add fields to a request that aren't present in the visual web form. Avoid the mistake of assuming that data not visible in the user interface is safe from modification; attackers can see and modify every part of an HTTP request.
lesson.fix: To fix this, first ensure that all active sessions are revoked (invalidated) immediately when a user's status changes to 'blocked' or 'deactivated'. Second, use an allow-list (a list of safe fields) when updating user data to prevent Mass Assignment. Instead of 'user.update(params)', use a method that only accepts specific fields: 'user.update(name: params[:name], bio: params[:bio])'. This ensures that sensitive fields like 'status' can only be changed by authorized administrative processes, never by the user's own profile update request.
